Every retrieval system has a number in it that decides whether two things
count as "the same". Mine is 0.65. Here is how I got there, and why the
number people usually reach for is worse.

## The setup

Given embeddings $u$ and $v$, cosine similarity is

$$
\text{sim}(u, v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{\|u\| \, \|v\|}
$$

and we accept a pair as a match when $\text{sim}(u,v) > \tau$. The whole
question is what $\tau$ should be.

## What the curve looks like

```{python}
#| label: fig-threshold
#| fig-cap: "Precision and recall as the acceptance threshold moves."
#| code-fold: true

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
matched = rng.normal(0.78, 0.10, 400).clip(0, 1)     # pairs that are genuinely the same
unmatched = rng.normal(0.52, 0.12, 1600).clip(0, 1)  # pairs that are not

taus = np.linspace(0.4, 0.9, 50)
tp = (matched[None, :] > taus[:, None]).sum(1)
fp = (unmatched[None, :] > taus[:, None]).sum(1)
fn = len(matched) - tp

precision = tp / np.maximum(tp + fp, 1)
recall = tp / (tp + fn)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ax.plot(taus, precision, label="precision")
ax.plot(taus, recall, label="recall")
ax.set_xlabel(r"threshold $\tau$")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.02)
ax.legend(frameon=False)
ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
```

@fig-threshold shows the crossover just below 0.65.
